title: Cycles and inversions
key_idea: Every permutation $w \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ has a unique cycle decomposition. The Stirling numbers $c(n,k)$ count permutations by number of cycles, and $\sum_k c(n,k)t^k = t(t+1)\cdots(t+n-1)$. Inversions $(i>j$ but $w_i < w_j)$ are encoded by the inversion table, giving a bijection $\mathfrak{S}_n \leftrightarrow \mathcal{T}_n$, and $\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_n} q^{\text{inv}(w)} = [n]!_q$.
summary: Stanley develops the cycle decomposition of permutations and its standardization (the hat map $w \mapsto \hat{w}$ converting cycles to words). The main result is Proposition 1.3.7: $\sum_k c(n,k)t^k = t(t+1)\cdots(t+n-1)$, proved four ways. Inversions give a bijection between $\mathfrak{S}_n$ and the product set $[0,n-1]\times\cdots\times[0,0]$, yielding the $q$-analogue $\sum q^{\text{inv}(w)} = [n]!_q$.

notation.description: Signless Stirling number of first kind: # permutations of $[n]$ with $k$ cycles
Number of inversions of $w$: $\#\{(i,j): i<j, w_i>w_j\}$
Word obtained by erasing parentheses from standard cycle form of $w$

definitions.statement:
Every permutation $w \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ decomposes uniquely into disjoint cycles. The **standard form** writes cycles so that each cycle begins with its largest element, and cycles are ordered with their largest elements increasing left to right. Example: $w = (3\,1)(5\,4\,2)$ is standard since $3 < 5$.

The map $w \mapsto \hat{w}$ erases parentheses from the standard form to give a word in $\mathfrak{S}_n$.

The **inversion table** of $w = w_1\cdots w_n \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ is $I(w) = (a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ where $a_i = \#\{j < i : w_j > w_i\}$ (equivalently, $a_i$ is the number of elements larger than $i$ that appear to the left of $i$ in $w$). Then $0 \leq a_i \leq n-i$, so $I(w) \in \mathcal{T}_n = [0,n-1]\times[0,n-2]\times\cdots\times[0,0]$.

propositions.title: Hat map bijection
propositions.statement: (a) The map $w \mapsto \hat{w}$ is a bijection $\mathfrak{S}_n \to \mathfrak{S}_n$. (b) Under this bijection, $w$ has $k$ cycles if and only if $\hat{w}$ has exactly $k$ left-to-right maxima (positions $i$ where $w_i > w_j$ for all $j < i$).
propositions.proof_sketch: The standard form is a deterministic procedure on cycles, so $\hat{w}$ determines $w$ (the left-to-right maxima mark cycle starts). Reversing: given a word, find its left-to-right maxima, insert parentheses before each to recover the cycle form.

propositions.title: Count by cycle type
propositions.statement: The number of permutations $w \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ of cycle type $(c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_n)$ (where $c_i = $ number of cycles of length $i$) is $$\frac{n!}{1^{c_1}c_1!\cdot 2^{c_2}c_2! \cdots n^{c_n}c_n!}.$$
propositions.proof_sketch: Write all $n!$ permutations as cycle products. A cycle of length $i$ can be written $i$ ways (cyclic rotations), and there are $c_i!$ ways to order the cycles of length $i$. Dividing by these symmetries gives the formula.

propositions.title: Rising factorial formula for Stirling numbers
propositions.proof_sketch:
**Proof 1 (semi-combinatorial):** Induction using Lemma 1.3.6 (recurrence for $c(n,k)$). The RHS satisfies the same recurrence as $c(n,k)$ and the same initial conditions.

**Proof 2 (cycle indicator):** Substitute $t_i = t$ for all $i$ in Theorem 1.3.3 to get $\sum_{n\geq 0} Z_n x^n = e^{t(x+x^2/2+\cdots)} = (1-x)^{-t}$. Expand to recover the rising factorial.

**Proof 3 (bijection):** The LHS counts pairs $(w, f)$ with $w \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ and $f: C(w) \to [t]$ (a coloring of cycles). There are $t^k$ colorings of a permutation with $k$ cycles. For $t \in \mathbb{P}$, the RHS also counts such pairs: choosing an element of $[t]$ for each of $n$ successive insertions.

**Proof 4 (bijection with pairs):** Stanley's bijection with pairs $(S, f)$ where $S \subseteq [n-1]$ and $f: S \to [n-1]$ with $f(i) \leq i$.

propositions.title: Inversion table and cycles
propositions.statement: The number of integer sequences $(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ with $0 \leq a_i \leq n-i$ and exactly $k$ of the $a_i$ equal to $0$ is $c(n,k)$.

propositions.title: Inversion table bijection
propositions.statement: The map $I: \mathfrak{S}_n \to \mathcal{T}_n = \{0,\ldots,n-1\}\times\{0,\ldots,n-2\}\times\cdots\times\{0\}$ sending $w$ to its inversion table is a bijection.
propositions.proof_sketch: The inversion table $(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ satisfies $0\leq a_i \leq n-i$, so $|\mathcal{T}_n| = n!$ and injectivity follows from reconstructability: insert elements $n, n-1, \ldots, 1$ in order, with $a_i$ elements to the left of $i$ at the time $i$ is inserted.

propositions.title: Inversions are preserved by inversion
propositions.proof_sketch: $(i,j)$ is an inversion of $w$ (i.e., $i<j$ and $w_i > w_j$) iff $(w_j, w_i)$ is an inversion of $w^{-1}$. This is a bijection between inversions of $w$ and inversions of $w^{-1}$.

theorems.title: Cycle indicator generating function
theorems.statement: Let $Z_n = Z_n(t_1,\ldots,t_n) = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_n} t^{\text{type}(w)}$ be the cycle indicator (where $t^{\text{type}(w)} = t_1^{c_1}\cdots t_n^{c_n}$). Then $$\sum_{n\geq 0} Z_n x^n = \exp\!\left(t_1 x + \frac{t_2 x^2}{2} + \frac{t_3 x^3}{3} + \cdots\right).$$
theorems.proof_sketch: Take the log of both sides. The count of permutations of type $(c_1,\ldots,c_n)$ from Proposition 1.3.2 factors into contributions from each cycle length, giving the exponential of a sum over cycle lengths.

corollaries.title: Left-to-right maxima and Stirling numbers
corollaries.statement: The number of $w \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ with exactly $k$ left-to-right maxima is $c(n,k)$.
corollaries.proof_sketch: Follows from Proposition 1.3.1(b) and the definition of $c(n,k)$: $\hat{w}$ has $k$ left-to-right maxima iff $w$ has $k$ cycles.

corollaries.title: $q$-analogue of $n!$
corollaries.proof_sketch: Via the bijection $I: \mathfrak{S}_n \to \mathcal{T}_n$, $\text{inv}(w) = \sum_i a_i$ (since $a_i$ counts inversions involving position $i$). Since the $a_i$ are independent with $0 \leq a_i \leq n-i$, the generating function factors as claimed.

examples.title: Building a permutation from $(S, f)$ data
examples.content: Let $n=9, k=4$ and $S=\{1,3,4,6,8\}$, $f(1)=1, f(4)=1, f(6)=3, f(8)=6$. Recover $w \in \mathfrak{S}_9$ with 4 cycles from the bijection in Proof 3 of Proposition 1.3.7.
examples.solution: The bijection maps $(S, f)$ to a permutation by placing $i$ into a new cycle whenever $i-1 \notin S$ and extending the cycle through $f$. Following the procedure for $n=9, k=4$ yields $w = (2)(4)(7\,5\,3)(9\,1\,6\,8)$.

examples.title: Inversion table example
examples.content: The sequence $(4,8,5,0,7,5,2,4,1)$ encodes which of $1,\ldots,9$ appears where. Recover the permutation.
examples.solution: Reading off: $a_1=4, a_2=8, \ldots$ — these are the positions of inversions. Insert elements $9,8,\ldots,1$ using the inversion table to recover the word $w$.

hints: Use the bijection with $\mathcal{T}_n$ and compute $\sum \sum_i a_i$.

text_passages.text: Every permutation $w \in \mathfrak{S}_n$ decomposes uniquely into disjoint cycles. Stanley's **standard form** imposes a canonical ordering: write each cycle starting with its largest element, order cycles by increasing largest element.

text_passages.label: Definition — Cycle decomposition and $\hat{w}$
text_passages.preview: Standard form puts largest element first in each cycle, cycles in increasing order of maxima. $\hat{w}$ erases parentheses, giving a bijection $\mathfrak{S}_n \to \mathfrak{S}_n$.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.3.1 — Hat map bijection
text_passages.preview: The map $w \mapsto \hat{w}$ is a bijection on $\mathfrak{S}_n$, with $w$ having $k$ cycles iff $\hat{w}$ has $k$ left-to-right maxima.

text_passages.text: Stirling numbers and the rising factorial

Let $c(n,k) = \#\{w \in \mathfrak{S}_n : w \text{ has } k \text{ cycles}\}$ (signless Stirling numbers of the first kind). The main theorem is that $\sum_k c(n,k)t^k$ equals the rising factorial $t(t+1)\cdots(t+n-1)$.

text_passages.label: Theorem 1.3.3 — Cycle indicator GF
text_passages.preview: $\sum_{n\geq 0} Z_n x^n = \exp(t_1x + t_2x^2/2 + \cdots)$. Specializing $t_i = t$ gives $(1-x)^{-t}$ and the rising factorial.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.3.7 — Rising factorial
text_passages.preview: $\sum_{k=0}^n c(n,k)t^k = t(t+1)\cdots(t+n-1)$. Stanley gives four proofs: recurrence, GF, bijection with colored cycles, bijection with pairs $(S,f)$.

text_passages.label: Definition — Inversion table
text_passages.preview: $I(w) = (a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ where $a_i = \#\{j<i : w_j > w_i\}$. Always $0 \leq a_i \leq n-i$.

text_passages.label: Proposition 1.3.12 — Inversion table bijection
text_passages.preview: $I: \mathfrak{S}_n \to \mathcal{T}_n = [0,n-1]\times\cdots\times[0,0]$ is a bijection. Since $|\mathcal{T}_n|=n!$, this accounts for all permutations.

text_passages.label: Corollary 1.3.13 — $q$-factorial
text_passages.preview: $\sum_{w\in\mathfrak{S}_n} q^{\text{inv}(w)} = (1+q)(1+q+q^2)\cdots(1+\cdots+q^{n-1}) = [n]!_q$. The $q$-factorial counts permutations by inversions.
